items.stem: Define the term 'copyright'.
items.answer: A legal right that protects the creator of an original work, such as software, music or text, from it being copied, distributed or adapted without permission.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: A legal right that protects the creator of an original work, such as software, music or text, from it being copied, distributed or adapted without permission. [2]

items.stem: Explain why copyright legislation is needed for software.
items.answer: Software is easy and cheap to copy; without protection developers would lose income from their investment, so there would be less incentive to create new software.
items.markingKey: 1 mark easy to copy; 1 mark lost income; 1 mark less incentive to innovate. [3]

items.stem: Explain two effects of software piracy on software companies.
items.answer: Loss of sales revenue; less money for development and support; higher prices for legitimate customers; jobs lost.
items.markingKey: 2 × (1 mark effect, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Tariq works in the marketing team of MetroBus in Mumbai, which develops software and produces promotional videos. Describe two methods used to prevent illegal copying of software.
items.answer: Product keys/activation; dongles; digital rights management; holograms on packaging; online licence checks.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Hana works in the marketing team of Silverline Couriers in Cape Town, which develops software and produces promotional videos. (a) Describe what copyright legislation allows the owner to control. (b) Explain why the material found online cannot simply be used.
items.answer: (a) Copying, distributing, adapting, performing, renting or broadcasting the work. (b) It is protected by copyright; permission/licence is needed or it must be royalty-free/Creative Commons with attribution.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per right, max 2. [2] (b) 1 mark copyright; 1 mark need permission/licence. [2]

items.stem: SwiftCar Rentals, a car rental company in Kuala Lumpur, sells its own software and is making a promotional video using music and images found online. Discuss whether copyright laws are effective in protecting digital content produced by organisations such as SwiftCar Rentals.
items.answer: Points for: legal action possible; deters large-scale copying; supports licensing income. Points against / limitations: digital content is copied easily and globally; enforcement across countries is difficult; DRM can annoy genuine customers. Conclusion: copyright law is necessary but must be supported by technical protection and affordable legal options.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks points developed and applied with a conclusion. Indicative content — for: legal action possible; deters large-scale copying; supports licensing income. Against: digital content is copied easily and globally; enforcement across countries is difficult; DRM can annoy genuine customers. Conclusion may argue: copyright law is necessary but must be supported by technical protection and affordable legal options. [4]

items.stem: Define the term 'single-user licence'.
items.answer: A licence that allows the software to be installed and used by one user, or on one computer, only.

items.stem: Explain the difference between freeware and open-source software.
items.answer: Freeware is free to use but the source code is not available and it cannot be modified; open-source software makes its source code available to be studied, modified and shared.

items.stem: Explain why a large organisation might choose a site licence rather than many single-user licences.

items.stem: FreshFarm Foods in Karachi needs software for 80 computers. A single-user licence costs $150; a multi-user licence for up to 50 users costs $2,500; a site licence for unlimited computers costs $3,000. Calculate the cost of each option and state the cheapest.
items.answer: single $12,000; multi-user $5,000; site $3,000; cheapest: a site licence
items.markingKey: single: 80 × 150 = $12,000 [1]; multi-user: 2 × 2,500 = $5,000 [1]; site $3,000; cheapest: a site licence [1]. [3]

items.stem: Identify the type of licence or software in each case and describe its terms: (1) A user downloads a game that can be played free for 14 days, then must be paid for. (2) A developer downloads a web server and edits its source code.
items.answer: (1) shareware — the software can be tried free for a limited period or with limited features; payment is then needed. (2) open-source licence — the source code is available and can be modified and shared under the licence terms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each type, 1 mark each description. [4]

items.stem: MetroBus in Mexico City has 120 computers in three buildings and needs a new office software package. (a) Explain what is meant by shareware. (b) Explain two ways the software company may try to prevent piracy.
items.answer: (a) Software that can be used free for a trial period or with limited features before payment. (b) Product keys; online activation; dongles; DRM.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark trial; 1 mark payment needed after. [2] (b) 2 × (1 mark method, 1 mark explanation). [4]

items.stem: Which term is described here? "A set of rules, agreed by users, stating how an organisation's IT systems and internet access may and may not be used."
options: fair use / fair dealing
hacking
acceptable use policy (AUP)
multi-user licence
items.answer: acceptable use policy (AUP)
items.markingKey: This describes acceptable use policy (AUP).

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'ethics' and 'plagiarism'.
items.answer: ethics: Moral principles about what is right and wrong that guide how people behave, including how they use IT. plagiarism: Presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own without acknowledging the source.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: ethics correctly described; 1 mark: plagiarism correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain two ways a school can detect or reduce plagiarism. (b) Explain why plagiarism is considered unethical even when it is not illegal.
items.answer: (a) Use plagiarism-detection software that compares work with online sources; teach referencing; set personalised tasks; ask students to explain their work. (b) It is dishonest: it takes credit for another person's work and misleads the reader or teacher about the author's abilities.
items.markingKey: (a) 2 × (1 mark method, 1 mark explanation). [4] (b) 1 mark dishonest/credit; 1 mark misleading. [2]

items.stem: Summit Engineering in Lisbon is writing an acceptable use policy after finding personal use of work computers and copied work in reports. Explain the difference between unethical and illegal behaviour, using an example from IT.
items.answer: Illegal breaks the law (e.g. hacking); unethical is morally wrong but may be legal (e.g. reading a colleague's screen, plagiarism).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each with example. [2]

items.stem: GreenLeaf Pharmacy in Riyadh is writing an acceptable use policy after finding personal use of work computers and copied work in reports. (a) Explain what is meant by plagiarism and why it is a problem. (b) Explain the difference between unethical and illegal behaviour, using an example from IT.
items.answer: (a) Using others' work without credit; dishonest; work does not show the student's ability; may break copyright. (b) Illegal breaks the law (e.g. hacking); unethical is morally wrong but may be legal (e.g. reading a colleague's screen, plagiarism).
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark meaning; 1 mark problem. [2] (b) 1 mark each with example. [2]

items.stem: Define the term 'fair use / fair dealing'.
items.answer: Limited use of copyright material without permission for purposes such as criticism, review, research or teaching, with acknowledgement.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Limited use of copyright material without permission for purposes such as criticism, review, research or teaching, with acknowledgement. [2]

items.stem: Describe the difference between 'software piracy' and 'copyright'.
items.answer: software piracy: Illegally copying, distributing or using software without a valid licence. copyright: A legal right that protects the creator of an original work, such as software, music or text, from it being copied, distributed or adapted without permission.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: software piracy correctly described; 1 mark: copyright correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Copyright protects software developers' income. Reason (R): The buyer does not own the copyright. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
items.markingKey: A and R are both true statements, but R does not explain A.

items.stem: Nadia works in the marketing team of Harbour Bank in Mumbai, which develops software and produces promotional videos. Describe what copyright legislation allows the owner to control.
items.answer: Copying, distributing, adapting, performing, renting or broadcasting the work.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per right, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Mei works in the marketing team of Silverline Couriers in Jakarta, which develops software and produces promotional videos. Explain why the material found online cannot simply be used.
items.answer: It is protected by copyright; permission/licence is needed or it must be royalty-free/Creative Commons with attribution.
items.markingKey: 1 mark copyright; 1 mark need permission/licence. [2]

items.stem: SwiftCar Rentals, a car rental company in Cape Town, sells its own software and is making a promotional video using music and images found online. (a) Explain why the material found online cannot simply be used. (b) Describe two methods used to prevent illegal copying of software.
items.answer: (a) It is protected by copyright; permission/licence is needed or it must be royalty-free/Creative Commons with attribution. (b) Product keys/activation; dongles; digital rights management; holograms on packaging; online licence checks.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark copyright; 1 mark need permission/licence. [2] (b) 1 mark each, max 2. [2]

items.stem: Freya works in the marketing team of Delta Water Utility in Mexico City, which develops software and produces promotional videos. (a) Describe what copyright legislation allows the owner to control. (b) Explain why the material found online cannot simply be used.
items.answer: (a) Copying, distributing, adapting, performing, renting or broadcasting the work. (b) It is protected by copyright; permission/licence is needed or it must be royalty-free/Creative Commons with attribution.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per right, max 2. [2] (b) 1 mark copyright; 1 mark need permission/licence. [2]

items.stem: Samuel works in the marketing team of Delta Water Utility in Muscat, which develops software and produces promotional videos. Discuss whether copyright laws are effective in protecting digital content produced by organisations such as Delta Water Utility.
items.answer: Points for: legal action possible; deters large-scale copying; supports licensing income. Points against / limitations: digital content is copied easily and globally; enforcement across countries is difficult; DRM can annoy genuine customers. Conclusion: copyright law is necessary but must be supported by technical protection and affordable legal options.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks developed points on one or both sides; 5-6 marks balanced, applied discussion with a justified conclusion. Indicative content — for: legal action possible; deters large-scale copying; supports licensing income. Against: digital content is copied easily and globally; enforcement across countries is difficult; DRM can annoy genuine customers. Conclusion may argue: copyright law is necessary but must be supported by technical protection and affordable legal options. [6]

items.stem: Define the term 'freeware'.
items.answer: Software that is free to use but is still protected by copyright, so users cannot modify it or sell it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: the key idea; 1 mark: further detail or a correct example. Model: Software that is free to use but is still protected by copyright, so users cannot modify it or sell it. [2]

items.stem: Distinguish between 'multi-user licence' and 'single-user licence'.
items.answer: multi-user licence: A licence that allows a stated number of users to use the software, often at the same time (concurrently). single-user licence: A licence that allows the software to be installed and used by one user, or on one computer, only.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: multi-user licence correctly described; 1 mark: single-user licence correctly described (a comparison is needed for full marks). [2]

items.stem: Assertion (A): Freeware cannot legally be sold by the user. Reason (R): One fee covers every computer at the site. Which option is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
items.answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
items.markingKey: A and R are both true statements, but R does not explain A.

items.stem: Noah, the IT manager at Nova Telecom in Singapore, is reviewing how the organisation licenses its software. Describe the difference between a single-user and a multi-user licence.
items.answer: Single-user: one user/computer; multi-user: a set number of users, often concurrent.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each. [2]

items.stem: Peak Fitness in Seoul needs software for 20 computers. A single-user licence costs $120; a multi-user licence for up to 50 users costs $1,500; a site licence for unlimited computers costs $3,000. Calculate the cost of each option and state the cheapest.
items.answer: single $2,400; multi-user $1,500; site $3,000; cheapest: multi-user licences
items.markingKey: single: 20 × 120 = $2,400 [1]; multi-user: 1 × 1,500 = $1,500 [1]; site $3,000; cheapest: multi-user licences [1]. [3]

items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each. [2] (b) 1 mark trial; 1 mark payment needed after. [2]

items.stem: Arjun, the IT manager at BlueWave Supermarkets in Cairo, is reviewing how the organisation licenses its software. Evaluate whether BlueWave Supermarkets should use freeware and open-source software instead of buying licences.
items.answer: Points for: saves licence costs; open source can be adapted; legal to share. Points against / limitations: less support; compatibility; training costs; may lack features; freeware may contain adverts or be discontinued. Conclusion: a mix is common; key business systems often justify paid licences with support.
items.markingKey: Levels marking: 1-2 marks basic points; 3-4 marks developed points on one or both sides; 5-6 marks balanced, applied discussion with a justified conclusion. Indicative content — for: saves licence costs; open source can be adapted; legal to share. Against: less support; compatibility; training costs; may lack features; freeware may contain adverts or be discontinued. Conclusion may argue: a mix is common; key business systems often justify paid licences with support. [6]

items.stem: Which action is plagiarism?
options: Quoting a website and listing it in a bibliography
Copying paragraphs from a website into an essay without a reference
Writing an essay in your own words
Asking a teacher for feedback
items.answer: Copying paragraphs from a website into an essay without a reference
items.markingKey: Copying paragraphs from a website into an essay without a reference. Using others' work without acknowledgement is plagiarism.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Explain two ways a school can detect or reduce plagiarism. (b) Explain why organisations ask employees to sign an acceptable use policy.

items.stem: Teachers at Horizon Travel in Lima have noticed that several students' assignments contain identical paragraphs from a website. Discuss whether monitoring employees' use of the internet is justified for Horizon Travel.
items.answer: Points for: protects security; enforces the AUP; reduces time wasting; legal compliance. Points against / limitations: invasion of privacy; reduces trust and morale; cost of monitoring; staff may feel they are not trusted. Conclusion: monitoring can be justified if it is proportionate, transparent and explained in the AUP.

Against: invasion of privacy; reduces trust and morale; cost of monitoring; staff may feel they are not trusted. Conclusion may argue: monitoring can be justified if it is proportionate, transparent and explained in the AUP. [4]
